### Sunday Closes With a Boy Pulled Alive From Dymer's Rubble, a Russian Corvette Sunk at Her Berth in Benghazi, and the Futures Up Two Percent at the Turn of the Log

Filed as: Edition No. 80 — The Midnight Watch · 2026-11-23T00:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-23-midnight-watch.html

The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Sunday Closes With a Boy Pulled Alive From Dymer’s Rubble, a Russian Corvette Sunk at Her Berth in Benghazi, and the Futures Up Two Percent at the Turn of the Log

 The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a child alive in the rubble and a count still rising around him; a warship sunk at a foreign berth a thousand miles from the war’s own sea; a summit’s failure given its mechanism; a claim about two radars that no capital has answered; a strait counted at two; and a market that fell all week and opened its futures rising.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Monday, November 23, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 79, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Sunday, in Edition No. 78, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Sunday, in Edition No. 76, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Sunday, and in Edition No. 75, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Sunday. The Sunday Review of Reviews, collected on Sunday, stands in the Weekend Features. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Sunday Settled, What It Left Open

Sunday settled a rescue, a sinking, and a market’s direction at the reopening—and left a town’s toll, a warship’s attackers, and two claimed radars open at the turn of the log. In Dymer, north of Kyiv, rescuers pulled a seven-year-old boy alive from the rubble of the five-storey building a drone destroyed before dawn, nearly 14 hours after the strike, in the rescue account filed below; the confirmed toll stands at four in the President’s word, in the toll account filed below, and at nine in the regional head’s later word, in the relayed account filed below, with the search still running at the stamp. At Benghazi, the Russian corvette Merkury capsized and sank at her berth after two sea drones struck her in the early hours, in the sinking account filed below, and a second ship was hit off the port in the evening. In Antalya, the first full account of the summit’s collapse lays the failure to one delegation’s access and a fixed position, in the post-mortem account filed below. The futures reopened at 1800 Eastern up across the board and rose through the evening, in the reopening account filed below. The desk takes the files in that order.

What Sunday settled is the boy’s rescue; the Merkury’s loss, established by satellite imagery and two governments’ statements; the Sparta II’s tow out of Finnish waters, completed on Sunday night in the Journal’s account; the Antalya outcome’s mechanism, in the negotiators’ own telling; the strait’s Sunday at two crossings in the visible counter; and the futures’ direction at the reopening. What it left open is the rest: Dymer’s final count, who sent the drones to Benghazi in that capital’s own word, the radars at Al-Riffa and Awali, the mines claimed in the Gulf of Oman, and Monday’s cash open, on a week that begins with a council in Brussels.

Libya at Midnight: A Corvette Sunk at Her Berth, a Second Ship Hit by Evening, and No Claim From Kyiv

Sunday’s largest new file opened before dawn in a port that is not in the war. The Merkury, a Steregushchiy-class corvette of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, was berthed at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya when two explosive-laden sea drones struck her in the early hours of Sunday, at least four more drones intercepted and destroyed, in the sinking account above and in the base account filed below. Satellite images showed most of the warship capsized and submerged, with only her bow remaining above water, in the sinking account; the imagery company Vantor identified the vessel as a Russian navy corvette, and imagery taken Sunday showed most of her capsized and sunk, smoke rising from part of her superstructure and debris scattered along the pier, in the imagery account filed below. Ten people, Russian and Libyan nationals, suffered minor injuries and were receiving treatment in Benghazi, in the medical sources carried in the sinking account and in the London account filed below; two medical sources in the first wire account said no deaths had been reported, in the wire account filed below, against local sources’ word, late on Sunday, of an unknown number of Libyan and Russian nationals killed, in the imagery account. The desk prints both and merges neither.

The official words are these. Libya’s eastern-based government said a preliminary investigation indicated the explosion occurred aboard a Russian ship docked at the port and that a drone attack was suspected; the vessel had stopped to refuel and resupply on her way back to Russia under maritime cooperation agreements, in the wire account. The same government said it has launched a joint investigation with Russia to uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it, in the imagery account. The initial investigation’s finding, in the base account, is that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya. Ukraine’s security service is widely believed to be responsible, in the London account, and a military source said the strike was carried out by the SBU, in the New York account filed below. Kyiv itself has claimed nothing in any account in the file. Libya’s Tripoli-based government said it was following the reports with grave concern about the danger of exposing the country’s civilian ports to external conflict, in the imagery account. The ship’s own recent work stands in the New York account: she had been stationed in Benghazi for several days after escorting a convoy of cargo vessels used to transport military supplies.

The file widened before it closed. Hours after the corvette was struck, a second drone attack hit a Maltese-flagged commercial ship off the coast of Benghazi, in the wire account; the Health Ministry of the Benghazi-based administration said the injured crew members had been rescued and were receiving treatment, in the imagery account, and Libyan naval and air forces intercepted more than 20 drone boats off Benghazi on Sunday evening, in the military sources carried in the sinking account. The Baltic file closed in the same hours at the other end of the continent: working with Finnish and Estonian authorities, Russia managed to tow the Sparta II out of Finnish waters on Sunday night, in the two-ships account filed below, and Kaliningrad’s governor wrote that there is no threat to the region’s supplies, in the same account. The tow’s weather warning stands in the tow account filed below: rain, sleet and stronger winds expected on Sunday night and Monday, named by Finland’s sea safety officer as a concern before the tow began. Two Russian ships struck in one weekend, in the Baltic and in the Mediterranean, neither claim answered by Kyiv in the file. Settled: the Merkury’s loss and the Sparta II’s departure. Open: the second ship’s state, the joint investigation, and responsibility in Kyiv’s word.

Ukraine at Midnight: A Boy Alive at Fourteen Hours, a Toll Counted Three Ways, and a Search Still Running

Dymer’s day ended with the fact the whole file had waited for. A seven-year-old boy, named David, was pulled alive from beneath the collapsed concrete of the five-storey building on Sunday evening, almost 14 hours after the Shahed drone struck at about 5 a.m. while residents slept, in the rescue account above. Rescuers found him after discovering personal belongings recognised by his relatives; he spoke to them without panicking and repeatedly assured them he was all right—“Don’t rush, I’m fine”—in the Interior Ministry chief Ivan Vyhivskyi’s telling, in the same account, and he was taken for treatment in stable condition. President Zelensky confirmed the rescue on Sunday evening and warned that the search was far from over, in the same account: more than 130 emergency personnel are at the site with heavy machinery, canine teams and bomb-disposal experts, in the toll account, and the operation will continue until there is complete information about every single person, in the President’s words in the rescue account. The rescuers are also investigating witness reports of a telephone call from a woman believed to be under the rubble, in both accounts.

The toll does not stand in one figure at the stamp, and the desk prints the count as it stands. The confirmed death toll has risen to four, in the President’s word, in the toll account, which adds that roughly ten people remain unaccounted for and that the Emergency Service has identified two of the dead: a woman born in 1978 and a boy born in 2008. The regional head, Timur Tkachenko, said the toll in Dymer has risen to nine, announced on Telegram, with one more body found in the rubble, in the relayed account, which counts at least 12 dead across the Kyiv region in the night’s attacks: nine in Dymer, two in Vyshneve, where a strike hit a supermarket and wounded eight, and one in Bila Tserkva, where a private house caught fire. The missing are counted in the same spread: 14 unaccounted for in the President’s first word, revised to 15 as teams pushed deeper, in the missing account filed below; nine people might still be trapped, in Mr. Vyhivskyi’s later word, in the rescue account; 11 still being searched for, including two children who are not responding or are not reachable, in the relayed account. The day’s interruption stands in the file: the search was suspended in the middle of the afternoon under a new aerial threat, three explosions were heard as rescuers and civilians took shelter, and work resumed under continuing alerts, in the day account filed below.

The week behind the day stands in the President’s own summary, in the missing account: the preceding seven days were one of the war’s most intense aerial stretches, with Russian forces firing thousands of drones, guided bombs and missiles across 20 Ukrainian regions, and Ukraine pressing allied governments to accelerate delivery of anti-ballistic interceptors. The standing files did not move: Thursday night’s toll at at least nine killed, the three Dnipro crossings in their two states with the Darnytskyi assessment still unpublished, and Kryvyi Rih’s toll at two dead and 60 wounded. The North Atlantic Council meets in Brussels on Monday with Dymer now in the file before it. Settled: the boy, alive. Open: the count, when the rubble is cleared.

Antalya at Midnight: The Post-Mortem Names Access, a Letter of 130 Countries, and a Fixed Position

The climate file’s last entry of the day is an account of how the failure was made. As COP31 drifted into record overtime, a negotiator from a small island state complained that a promised meeting with the talks’ Turkish and Australian presidents had been cancelled yet again, while Saudi officials had regular access, allowing them disproportionate influence at Antalya, according to negotiators from Europe, small island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa, in the post-mortem account above. Riyadh was at the forefront of resisting language on reducing reliance on fossil fuels, and that was chiefly why a political agreement could not be reached for the first time since 2009, the negotiators said, in the same account. The opposing coalition’s instrument stands in the same file: a letter backed by around 130 countries, saying any deal at Antalya must include mention of transitioning away from fossil fuels, sent to the presidency—and the revised text that emerged early on Sunday largely ignored it, still naming no fossil fuels and keeping strong language promoting carbon capture, in the same account. “It seems like we are negotiating with the Saudis,” Tuvalu’s climate minister, Maina Talia, said at the time, in the same account.

The principals’ closing words stand as the evening filed them, with two additions. The Secretary-General of the United Nations, Antonio Guterres, said he shares the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment, and that the take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more, in the Paris account filed below, which adds that the rejected text received support from Russia, China and the Arab countries. “This has been the worst ever COP and its collapse needs to be a wake up call for the world,” Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, said, in the collapse account filed below. The presidency’s last word is in the business account filed below: there is nothing to do, we did all that we could, and there will be no new text from now on. The absence that strengthened the fixed position is named in the post-mortem: no active United States engagement at Antalya, and no close United States–China coordination of the kind that brokered compromises at earlier conferences; the United States did not take part for the second year in a row, in the analysis account filed below. Settled: the outcome, and now its mechanism in the negotiators’ telling. Open: where the process goes next, which no account in the file answers.

The Gulf at Midnight: Two Injured Standing, a Claim Unanswered, and a Strait Counted at Two

Bahrain’s file ends Sunday exactly where the evening left its centre: unanswered. The Guards’ claim stands in its own words—two Patriot radars at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases struck in a combined missile and drone operation, in the Guards account filed below and in the agency account filed below, which also carries Iran’s own inconsistency: the Fars agency named the Shaikh Isa and Al Juffair bases in the minutes before the statement. Manama’s account stands against it: a purely civilian industrial site, two injured—a Bahraini citizen in stable condition and a Pakistani resident in critical condition—and the region’s condemnation joined in full through the day. The American word in the file remains the one word: no damage to American personnel or facilities in the region, in an official’s statement to CBS News, in the roundup account filed below, which is not a statement about the radars. One new Washington line stands in the file at the stamp, and it is about the next move, not the last one: the United States and Israel are weighing potential renewed strikes against Iran, Israel favors a joint operation, and President Trump has given no indication he will authorize such a move, in the CBS reporting carried in the Manama account filed below. Tehran’s standing offer also stands: the two-day plan to cease hostilities and reopen the strait is the sole proposal Iran has put forward and is still on the table, Deputy Foreign Minister Gharibabadi told reporters, in the agency account.

The strait’s Sunday is now closed in the visible counter, and it closes at the two crossings the midday file already carried: the Lolo Gate outbound at 0613 UTC and the Emily inbound at 1009 UTC, no tankers, with the seven-day figure at 55 crossings, an average of 7.9 a day, about 9 percent of the pre-crisis 84.8, in the strait count filed below. The second instrument counts its wider sea through the night: 26 ships in the 24 hours to 0231 UTC on Monday, 14 in and 12 out, with tankers carrying an estimated 0.82 million barrels out, in the monitor account filed below—whose Sunday-evening table again lists the tanker Khat Shekan outbound at 2331 UTC, the name the desk struck from the record on Sunday as a spoof transmission, and the desk does not restore it on the monitor’s word. A third instrument disagrees with both: five ships crossed on Saturday and none on Sunday, in the Kpler data cited by Reuters and published by Gulf Times, in the tracking account filed below. The mine claim in the Gulf of Oman and the Kharg convoy stand as the evening left them: claimed and unsailed. Monday opens at zero crossings in the counter’s first reading. Settled: the two injured, the condemnation, and Sunday’s two. Open: the radars, the mines, the convoy, and the true count.

The West Bank at Midnight: An Investigation Without Arrests, and Four Weeks on the Clock

The West Bank file did not move after the evening, and the desk records its standing as the day’s close. The attacks stand: at least a dozen cars torched and several homes vandalized across four villages in the night, no injuries reported, graffiti reading “Revenge” and “Death to Arabs” on the walls, in the Ramallah account filed below and in the villages account filed below. The state’s answer stands in its two parts: the military condemned the violence and dispatched soldiers and police to Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Masha’al, Kafr Malik and At-Tuwani, and the police opened an investigation and said they would enter the villages under military escort to collect evidence, in both accounts. No arrests have been announced, in the villages account. The word spoken in Jerusalem stands: “Jewish terrorism,” in Mr. Eisenkot’s words, with administrative detention and targeted operations urged against the assailants, and the violence laid to the policies of Mr. Ben-Gvir and Mr. Smotrich. Mr. Eisenkot has four more weeks to attempt to form a government, in the villages account. Settled: the attacks and the investigation’s opening. Open: its findings, and the government’s formation.

The Markets at Midnight: Futures Up Two Percent at the Reopening, a Coin Closed at $60,784, and Monday’s Tests Named

The week’s last market fact is a direction, and it is the opposite of the week’s. The futures reopened at 1800 Eastern, at the evening edition’s stamp, and rose from the first reading: just after 1800, S&P 500 futures were up 1.3 percent, Nasdaq 100 futures up 2 percent, and Dow futures up 0.8 percent, or nearly 400 points, in the reopening account above. The rise held and widened through the evening: at 2132 Eastern, Dow futures were up 1.54 percent, the S&P 500 futures up 1.96 percent and the Nasdaq-100 futures up 2.33 percent, in the late account filed below, which prints Friday’s closes beneath them—the Dow down 1.93 percent at 48,147.33, the S&P 500 down 3.70 percent at 6,910.39, the Nasdaq Composite down 5.28 percent at 22,617.73. The latest reading in the file is the strongest: Dow futures up 1.7 percent, S&P 500 futures up 2.35 percent and Nasdaq-100 futures up 3.1 percent, amid Oracle and South Korea news, in the futures account filed below, which names the evening’s supports: Oracle said its OpenAI funding is secured, and South Korean authorities moved to steady their markets after the worst week since March 2020. A futures reopening is a reading, not a session; the cash market that fell 10 percent on the week for the Nasdaq Composite has not yet spoken, and Japan is closed Monday for a holiday, thinning the Asian session the evening’s rise must cross.

The coin closes Sunday above its line on every reading in the file. On the exchange’s UTC day, November 22 closes at $60,783.58—open $60,215.78, high $61,669.99, low $58,768.51—in the closing account filed below; early in the American evening it stood at $60,785.36, up 1.15 percent, with Ethereum at $1,719.76, up 2.23 percent, in the evening account filed below.  The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 35 items.

 SubjectiveReuters — Saudi Arabia’s influence loomed large over failed COP31 dealAs the COP31 climate conference drifted into what proved to be record overtime, a negotiator from a small island state complained that a promised meeting with the talks’ Turkish and Australian presidents had been cancelled yet again. Saudi officials, meanwhile, had regular access, allowing them disproportionate influence at the Antalya conference, according to negotiators from Europe, small island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa. Riyadh was at the forefront of resisting language on reducing reliance on fossil fuels, the negotiators said, adding that was chiefly why a political agreement could not be reached for the first time since 2009. The European Union, several small island states, and other nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the oil, gas, and coal that scientists say drive global warming. Saudi Arabia and fellow members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries have long opposed climate language targeting fossil fuels. Several negotiators said Riyadh’s hand was strengthened at Antalya by the absence of active United States engagement at COP31 and the lack of close United States–China coordination that has helped broker compromises at previous COPs. Together the opposing coalition produced a letter, backed by around 130 countries, that said any deal at Antalya must include mention of transitioning away from fossil fuels, and sent it to the presidency; when the revised text finally emerged early on Sunday, it largely ignored the coalition letter, still had no mention of fossil fuels and kept strong language promoting carbon capture. “It seems like we are negotiating with the Saudis,” Maina Talia, Tuvalu’s climate minister, said at the time. As Sunday wore on, negotiators openly discussed the possibility that the talks could collapse without a political statement, and delegates were leaving Antalya to catch flights.

 SubjectiveCNN — Global climate summit collapses as countries fail to agree on moving away from fossil fuelsThe COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed Sunday as countries failed to agree to an overarching deal after more than two weeks of contentious negotiations. The breaking point was over the very cause of climate change itself: fossil fuels. The annual talks, which stretched deep into overtime over the weekend, hold the honor of being the longest COP in history and the first major breakdown since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009. At the final meeting intended to approve the so-called Antalya Pact on Sunday, it became clear there would not be the necessary consensus between the more than 190 countries at the talks to adopt the deal; these did not include the United States, which has pulled out of international climate action. The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway were among those that rejected it. Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s climate minister, said the bloc would not endorse a deal that does not even mention fossil fuels. COP31 president Murat Kurum acknowledged support was not there to gavel through the pact: “We have done our utmost,” he said, but “it is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document.” Experts criticized the conference as a stunning failure of leadership; “This has been the worst ever COP and its collapse needs to be a wake up call for the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the energy think tank Power Shift Africa.

 SubjectiveLe Monde — COP31: International community splits over phasing out fossil fuels and climate adaptation fundingOn Sunday, November 22, the world’s countries overwhelmingly rejected the “Antalya Pact,” a framework decision intended to send a strong political message to accelerate the fight against the climate catastrophe. After two weeks of negotiations, the longest COP in history ended without any significant progress, marking the biggest setback since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009. “I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” said United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. “The take-home message from COP31 is clear: The world must do much more to confront the climate crisis.” In the view of the European Union, Panama, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the group of least developed countries, the framework decision—which did not explicitly mention fossil fuels—fell far short of addressing the scale of the challenges. The text, however, received support from Russia, China, and the Arab countries. For the first time, the draft decision called for greater efforts to minimize both the scale and duration of the projected overshooting of the 1.5-degree global warming threshold.

 SubjectiveThe Associated Press, carried by Daily Fox News — Analysis: Yearslong fossil fuel disputes set stage for UN climate talks collapseGoing into this year’s United Nations climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low, but the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected: a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures. For the second year in a row, the United States, the world’s richest country and historically its largest polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the United States from climate negotiations. In the 30 years of climate negotiations, the one exception to the absence of the words fossil fuels from final agreements was the conference three years ago in Dubai, COP28, where the final decision encouraged countries to “transition away from fossil fuels”; fossil fuels were not mentioned in the final agreements in the following two conferences, and the current one, of course, had no final agreement. Earlier in the final week, Panama’s Juan Carlos Navarro was among those who pressed the point in the room.

 SubjectiveFox Business — UN climate summit collapses in Turkey over fossil fuels, carbon capture and climate financeUnited Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed on Sunday after the European Union and several other nations rejected a final draft agreement from co-hosts Turkey and Australia over its lack of explicit language on fossil fuels—the first time the annual summit has failed to adopt an overarching deal since Copenhagen in 2009. After running two days into overtime, Turkish COP31 President Murat Kurum told delegates at the closing plenary that there was no consensus and no further text would be offered: “There is nothing to do, we did all that we could. There will be no new text from now on.” Australia’s COP31 President of Negotiations, Chris Bowen, also addressed the outcome. At the heart of the breakdown was the agreement’s omission of fossil fuels; an unedited November 19 presidency draft made no explicit mention of fossil fuels, oil, coal or natural gas, referencing only the 2023 Dubai climate summit outcome. The draft leaned into industrial carbon capture, utilization and storage, proposing targets for it, and cited developing nations’ estimated climate finance needs at $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion through 2030, calling to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035—a target developing nations criticized for lacking a clear baseline.

The military said it also received reports of an attack on the Palestinian village of At-Tuwani in the southern West Bank near Hebron, and said it condemns acts of violence of this nature. Israeli police said on Sunday they would enter the Palestinian villages under military escort to collect evidence; police have not announced any arrests after the attacks.

 SubjectiveBarron’s — Stock Futures Are Rebounding After Last Week’s BloodbathJust after 6 p.m. Eastern time on Sunday, S&P 500 futures were up 1.3 percent, Nasdaq 100 futures were up 2 percent, and Dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose 0.8 percent, or nearly 400 points. The futures had reopened at 6 p.m. Eastern after the worst week in years for the cash markets.

The account carries Friday’s closes beneath the futures: the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 1.93 percent at 48,147.33, the S&P 500 down 3.70 percent at 6,910.39, and the Nasdaq Composite down 5.28 percent at 22,617.73.

### The Sparta II Goes Out Under Tow With Her Containers Still Warm, Dymer Counts Four Dead With Ten Still in the Rubble, and COP31 Ends in Antalya With No Deal and the Words Fossil Fuels Unwritten

Filed as: Edition No. 79 — The Evening Watch · 2026-11-22T18:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-22-evening-watch.html

The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 The Sparta II Goes Out Under Tow With Her Containers Still Warm, Dymer Counts Four Dead With Ten Still in the Rubble, and COP31 Ends in Antalya With No Deal and the Words Fossil Fuels Unwritten

 The evening file—the day’s developments whole, and the first considered responses from every side: a burning ship handed back across a border under tow, a rescue stopped by the threat that made it necessary, a condemnation joined by a region while the radars stay unanswered, a summit that ran longest and agreed to nothing, a factory’s missing counted three ways, and a coin holding its line at the hour the futures come back.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Sunday, November 22, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 78, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today, from Edition No. 76, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, from Edition No. 75, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, and from Edition No. 74, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Saturday. The Sunday Review of Reviews, collected this morning, stands in the Weekend Features. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the evening figures differ from the figures those editions carried, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Evening in Brief: A Tow Begun, a Rescue Halted, and a Summit Ended Without a Text

The day whole is a burning ship handed back across a maritime border, a rescue in Ukraine stopped by the threat that made it necessary, and a climate summit that ran longer than any before it and produced no agreement. The Sparta II, struck by two drones on Saturday west of Gogland island, went out of Finnish waters under tow on Sunday afternoon behind the Russian rescue vessel Murman, after seven vessels of three countries fought her fire through the night; her containers were still warm on the thermal cameras, no flames were visible from outside, and one of her 16 crew was slightly injured, in the tow account filed below and in the departure account filed below. In Dymer, north of Kyiv, a Russian drone destroyed part of a five-storey apartment building on Sunday morning; four people were killed in the region, about ten may still be trapped, 14 were out of contact in the President’s count, and the rescuers themselves had to stop and take shelter in the afternoon, in the Kyiv region account filed below. In Antalya, COP31 ended on Sunday with no overarching agreement: the European Union and other countries refused a final text that did not mention fossil fuels, and the conference president conceded there was no consensus, in the collapse account filed below. Bahrain’s file closed the day with its two injured standing, its condemnations joined by the Arab League, the Gulf Cooperation Council and the Arab Parliament, and the claimed Patriot radars still without an American word addressed to them. The desk takes the files in that order.

What the evening settled is the Sparta II’s tow and her departure from the Finnish responsibility area; the Dymer toll at four dead in the region, with its trapped and missing still counted two ways; the Antalya outcome, which is a non-outcome, stated in the principals’ own words; the regional condemnation of the Bahrain attack, joined in full; and the strait’s Sunday at two crossings in the visible counter, with Saturday corrected a third time, now to 14. What it left open is the rest: the radars, the rubble’s full count, the Kharg convoy’s sailing, a factory’s missing in Banten, and Monday’s open, on a week that begins with a council in Brussels.

The Baltic at Evening: Seven Vessels, One Tow, and a Handover at the Border

The Baltic file is the day’s one file that closes, and it closes with cooperation across the line the war drew. A Russian rescue vessel on Sunday began towing the Sparta II out of Finnish waters after two days of firefighting, Finland’s coast guard said, in the tow account above. “Thermal cameras show that some containers are warm, but the vessel is stable enough for towing to begin,” the coast guard said, and responsibility for the rescue transfers to Russia once the ship leaves Finnish waters, in the same account. The evening update carries the tow to its end inside the Finnish area: the Murman began towing on Sunday afternoon, the ship listing slightly and stable enough to move, no flames visible from outside and no fuel or hazardous-substance leaks detected; the Finnish patrol vessel Uisko, Estonia’s Kindral Kurvits and tugs operated by Alfons H&aring;kans supported the tow inside the responsibility area, the maritime and aviation restrictions were lifted, and the ship left both the economic zone and the environmental-damage area, ending the Border Guard’s mission, in the departure account.

The firefighting’s company is stated plainly in the file, and the desk prints it as it stands: of the seven vessels helping to fight the fire, two were Russian, two were Estonian and the rest were Finnish, in the tow account—the same three flags that stand on opposite sides of the war’s other files, working one burning ship in one sea. The crew’s account gains its last detail: the 16 were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship, and one crew member was slightly injured, in both accounts—the first injury in the Sparta II’s file, where the week’s earlier accounts carried none. The ship herself stands as the file has carried her: 121 metres, Russian-flagged, owned by Oboronlogistika, bound for Kaliningrad, damaged in international waters west of Gogland island, in Finland’s Defence Forces’ placing, corroborating an account by Russian officials, in the tow account. Finland’s attribution stands where Finland placed it—the strike was likely carried out by Ukraine—and Kyiv has claimed nothing in any account in the file, as at every earlier stamp. Settled: the tow, the handover, the crew at 16 with one slight injury, and the fire reduced to warm containers. Open: the cargo, the tow’s destination and arrival, and responsibility in Kyiv’s word.

Ukraine at Evening: Dymer’s Rubble, a Rescue Stopped at 1535, and a Call for Patriots Renewed

Sunday’s new Ukrainian file opened in the morning in the Vyshhorod district and was still open at the stamp. A Russian drone struck a five-storey apartment building in Dymer, a small town north of Kyiv, destroying part of the building and collapsing flats across its floors; the bodies of three people were found in the building, about ten people may still be trapped under the rubble, and at least four people were killed in the region’s drone attacks on Sunday in all, in the Kyiv region account above. Nine people were evacuated and the fire was contained, in the President’s words in the same account: “Part of a five-story apartment building has collapsed following a Russian drone attack. I thank our first responders for acting quickly.” Four people, including a teenager, were injured, in the same account; the oblast administration’s running count names two dead recovered from the building itself and four casualties, with a teenager and a 22-year-old woman injured in the district, in the rubble account filed below. The wire count stands at at least three killed and four wounded in the building, with nearly a dozen feared buried and 11 believed trapped in the Emergency Service’s earlier figure, in the wire account filed below. The President’s figure for the missing is the largest in the file: contact lost with 14 people after the morning attack, some of whom could have been under the rubble, in the rubble account.

The afternoon added the file’s hardest fact. At 3:35 p.m. local time the rescuers had to stop their search for survivors because of an incoming aerial threat; shortly after, three explosions rang through Dymer, footage showed an unidentified aerial object on fire falling from the sky, and civilians and rescuers took shelter in nearby buildings, in the Kyiv region account. The President renewed his call, in the day’s file, for the United States to approve deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles financed by allies. The standing files did not move, and the desk records them as standings: Thursday night’s toll at at least nine killed, the three Dnipro crossings in their two states—all closed in the BBC’s account, the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi restored in Kyiv’s—with the Darnytskyi assessment still unpublished, and Kryvyi Rih’s toll at two dead and 60 wounded. The North Atlantic Council meets in Brussels on Monday, with the Secretary General’s Warsaw guarantee of Saturday in the file before it and Dymer now in the same file. Settled: four dead in the region, nine evacuated, the fire contained, and the search interrupted. Open: the trapped, the missing, and the count when the rubble is cleared.

Bahrain at Evening: Two Injured Standing, a Region’s Condemnation Joined, and the Radars Still Unanswered

Bahrain’s evening file is the midday file with its diplomatic ring completed and its central question untouched. The injured stand as the Interior Ministry corrected them on Sunday: a Bahraini citizen with disabilities in stable condition and a Pakistani resident in critical condition, both in hospital, in the injured account filed below and in the condition account filed below. Manama’s answer to Tehran’s targeting claim is now in the file in terms: the Foreign Ministry dismissed the Guards’ account, saying the site hit was purely civilian and industrial, calling the attack a direct danger to civilians and a violation of the kingdom’s sovereignty, in the dismissal account filed below. The condemnation widened through the day in a stated order: Saudi Arabia and the Gulf Cooperation Council, in the midday file; then the Arab League, in its strongest condemnation, affirming full solidarity with Bahrain’s leadership, government and people and support for all sovereign measures the kingdom takes, and the Council’s Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi in the same terms, in the League account filed below; and the Arab Parliament, warning that the approach pushes the region toward a wider circle of confrontation and calling for an immediate halt, in the Parliament account filed below. Manama’s call on the Security Council—to halt such attacks, hold those responsible accountable and ensure compensation—stands from the midday file, with no date for any Council meeting in the evening file.

Tehran’s claim stands where it stood, with its code name: the Aerospace Force attacked two United States Patriot radars at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in a combined missile and drone operation, “Ya Umm al-Banin,” in response to violations of Iranian airspace by MQ-1 and MQ-9 drones, in the Guards account filed below. The American word in the evening file is the word the midday file carried, and no more: a United States official told CBS News the attacks caused no damage to American personnel or facilities in the region, in the injured account; Central Command, which denied the F-16 claim in full on Saturday—“Iran did not attack a US F-16 fighter aircraft yesterday, at all,” in the denial account filed below—has filed no located statement on the claimed radars, in the day-268 account filed below, whose cutoff is 0500 ET and which records none of the Guards’ claims as independently verified. The desk prints the standing exactly: the one American denial in the file answers a claim about a jet; the claim about the radars has no American answer in the file at the stamp. Settled: the two injured, the purely-civilian character of the site in Manama’s word, and the region’s condemnation. Open: the radars, the drones, and any Council date.

The Strait at Evening: Two Crossings on Sunday, Saturday Corrected a Third Time, and a Mine Claim in the Gulf of Oman

The strait’s Sunday closes at the level its week has made normal, and its Saturday closes at a third figure. Two identification-system-visible commercial ships crossed on Sunday, one inbound and one outbound, no tankers, as of 18:35 UTC, the most recent the cargo ship Emily, inbound at 10:09 UTC, in the strait count filed below—the same two the midday reading carried, with no crossing added in the afternoon hours. Saturday, November 21, now counts at 14 crossings, nine inbound and five outbound, three of them tankers, in the same count, against the 13 the midday file printed and the 12 the overnight file closed the day at: three readings of one day in one instrument, printed here in succession as the house prints its corrections. The seven-day figure stands at 57, 33 inbound and 24 outbound, 16 of them tankers, an average of 8.1 a day, about 10 percent of the pre-crisis 84.8, the status severely restricted, in the same count, which states plainly that it counts ships visible on the identification system and misses the ships sailing dark. The second instrument counts its wider sea to the evening: 23 ships in the 24 hours to 18:01 UTC, 11 in and 12 out, with tankers carrying an estimated 0.82 million barrels out, in the monitor account filed below, whose Sunday table again names two tankers—the Wisdom Star inbound and the Velos Turquoise outbound—on a day the visible counter counts at none.

The day’s new strait-adjacent claim is a mine claim, and the desk files it as a claim beside an unconnected report. Iran’s navy stated on Sunday that two supertankers hit naval mines and caught fire after entering a restricted area east of the strait, north of Ghanam Island, where the vessels had switched off their detection and navigation systems, and both vessels stopped moving after the collision, in the mines account filed below, which also carries the navy’s warning against reliance on what it called smugglers such as CENTCOM. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency confirmed on Sunday that it received a report of an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman, gave no further details, and said an investigation was underway; it remained unclear whether that report involved either of the tankers described by Iran, and no injuries were reported, in the same account. The file already holds a mine in this water: the navy’s claim that a tanker struck a mine east of the strait stands behind Saturday’s Torkel and Arina file, in the day-268 account, and the imagery digest carries the two ships as struck off Khasab under warnings 215-26 and 216-26. Whether Sunday’s two supertankers are those two ships retold, or two more, no account in the evening file establishes, and the desk does not merge them. The spoof stands struck from the record, as the midday file left it: the Khat-Shekan does not exist, in the spoof account filed below. The Kharg convoy stands staged and unsailed: more than 14 tankers gathered, no independent confirmation of any departure, in the convoy account filed below, with the blockade at 130 consecutive days as of Saturday in the same file. Settled: Sunday’s two, Saturday’s 14 in the latest reading, and the spoof. Open: the mines, the convoy, and the true count.

The West Bank at Evening: A Dozen Cars Burned, an Investigation Opened, and a Word Spoken in Jerusalem

The Middle East’s second file of the day opened before dawn in the villages around Ramallah and ran through Israel’s politics by evening. Settlers attacked Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank early on Sunday, starting fires and scrawling graffiti; burned-out vehicles and walls spray-painted with slogans such as “Revenge” stood in villages near Ramallah, no one immediately claimed responsibility, and no injuries were reported, in the Ramallah account filed below. At least a dozen cars were torched and several homes vandalized across the night, in the villages account filed below, which names Kufr Malik, Deir as-Sudan and Deir Abu Masha’al; the military’s own list of the areas its soldiers and police were dispatched to adds At-Tuwani, in the Ramallah account. Israeli police said they had opened an investigation, and the military condemned the violence, in the same account.

The responses are the evening’s substance, and the desk prints them in the order they stand. Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader asked to form a government, called the attacks “Jewish terrorism”: “extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations,” in the Ramallah account, and, in the villages account, “acts of Jewish terrorism, and we must call them by their name,” with a call for administrative detention and targeted operations against the assailants. He laid the violence to the policies of Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who he said had brought the area to the brink of anarchy, in both accounts. Ben-Gvir replied on X that the condemnation amounted to selling out to Arab parties, in the Ramallah account. Yousef Jabareen, chair of the Arab Joint List, said settler terrorism in the West Bank does not take place in a vacuum, in the villages account. The standing figure in the file is the United Nations’ count: 410 settler attacks related to the olive harvest since the beginning of September, in the same account. Mr. Eisenkot has four more weeks to attempt to form a government, in the villages account; the parliament was sworn in on November 10 with no new government, the caretaker prime minister remains in office, in the Ramallah account. Settled: the attacks, the burned cars, the investigation, and the word spoken. Open: the investigation’s findings, and the government’s formation.

Antalya at Evening: The Longest Summit Ends With No Pact, and the Two Words Are the Reason

The climate file closed on Sunday in Antalya, Turkey, and it closed without a text. International talks broke down in overtime over how to address fossil fuels; delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering electrification targets, adaptation finance, and how to respond to the planet’s approaching breach of a key warming threshold, in the wire account filed below. The talks ran two days longer than expected and became the longest climate conference in the history of the summits, in the same account; the collapse is the first major breakdown since Copenhagen in 2009, in the collapse account. At the final meeting called to approve the Antalya Pact, consensus was not there among the more than 190 countries present; the United States, which has withdrawn from the process, was not among them, in the collapse account. The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway were among those that rejected the deal, in the same account.

The reason is stated in the principals’ own words, and the desk prints them together. “We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change,” Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s climate minister speaking for the Union, said, in the finale account filed below; and, in the rift account filed below: “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuel either.” Mr. O’Brien left the room with Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra, in the wire account. The conference president, Murat Kurum, conceded the failure in the room: “We have done our utmost,” he said, but “it is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document,” in the collapse account. The drafting history stands in the same account: the first draft of the cover decision called for “the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”; every subsequent draft stripped the words out, against a push by more than 100 countries to keep them in. What did get signed stands beside the failure: more than 90 countries signed a pledge to ramp up the electrification of their economies, in the collapse account, and only $142 million in additional funding was pledged at the summit, in the wire account. Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who ran the negotiations, said the transition away from fossil fuels is happening regardless of what the agreements say, in the wire account. The analysis in the evening file adds the context the delegates themselves gave: the failure follows weak outcomes at recent conferences, the absence of a major power backing a positive outcome was named by the Caribbean group’s lead as a big issue, and the determination of the large oil producers, led by Saudi Arabia, to block the fossil-fuel language arguably reflected the scale of the transition already achieved, in the aftermath account filed below; the energy shock from the Iran war made developing countries more reluctant to limit investment in new supplies, in the rift account. Settled: no pact, no consensus, and the reason in two words. Open: where the process goes next, which no account in the file answers.

The World at Evening: A Capture Confirmed in Mexico City, a Factory’s Missing in Banten, and Two Standings in France

Mexico’s file reached its confirmed form over the weekend and stands complete at the stamp. Mexican special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” in Guasave, Sinaloa, on Friday night in an operation conducted with United States intelligence, and he was flown to Mexico City, in the capture account filed below. Four soldiers and seven gunmen were killed, in the same account; the Defense Ministry’s count of the operation’s dead is 11 in all, in the operation account filed below, which also records that the gunfire sent fans fleeing from a baseball game. Seven other alleged members of the organization were arrested, including its second-in-command, Germ&aacute;n “N,” alias “Seraf&iacute;n,” and its alleged financial operator, Jos&eacute; “N,” in the operation account. The man himself is stated plainly: 44 years old, on the FBI’s ten most-wanted list, under a United States indictment since 2012 with a $5 million reward, wanted in Mexico on organized-crime and drug-trafficking charges, his group controlling smuggling routes for fentanyl and other narcotics along the border, in the capture account. Security Secretary Omar Garc&iacute;a Harfuch called the capture an important step toward the pacification of Sinaloa, in the same account. The accused stand accused; no account in the file reports a plea or a court date.

Indonesia’s file is a count that has not finished. A fire swept the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in the Serang district of Banten province at 5 p.m. local time on Saturday; at least three workers are dead, in the Jakarta account filed below. About 300 workers were inside the compound and 65 were believed to be in the affected area; as of Sunday afternoon 24 had returned home and four were receiving medical treatment, while 37 remained unaccounted for, the company’s chief executive, Steven Wijaya, said at a joint news conference, in the same account. The second count in the file runs higher: 54 initially reported missing, 15 rescued including four injured, leaving 36 unaccounted for in the rescue agency’s arithmetic, while police and the owner placed the number of missing closer to 50, in the search account filed below, which also records seven body bags recovered and an identification process that could take two to three weeks, with the victims not identifiable by sight. Survivors told Indonesian media the flames originated from a cooling unit on the third floor; police said the cause remains under investigation, in the same account. The factory produces Milkita candies, exported to more than 40 countries, in the Jakarta account. Settled: the fire, its hour, and three dead. Open: the missing, counted at 36, 37 and near 50 in the file’s three arithmetics.

France’s two files stand at evening where the midday left them, and the desk records the standings once. The Miro G remains stranded off the Landes coast, ballast tanks filled, both main generators failed, the tug Abeille Bretagne standing off at about 900 metres with its 1,000-metre towline, no one aboard, no pollution detected, and refloating a matter of several days or longer, in the salvage account filed below. The police firearms law stands adopted, unpromulgated and un-referred in any account in the evening file, the Senate left’s promised referral to the Constitutional Council still a promise at the stamp. Spain’s campaign stands on its itinerary: Mr. Feij&oacute;o in Murcia today and C&aacute;diz on Monday, the Valencia count agreed at 12,000, the average at 30.9 against 27.9, and the vote on November 29. Sunday’s Review of Reviews stands in the Weekend Features, filed this morning. Settled: the standings. Open: the refloating, the referral, and the campaign’s last week.

The Markets at Evening: A Coin Above $60,000 at the Futures Hour, a Panic Index at Nine, and the Week’s Bill on the Table

The evening’s market fact is an hour: the futures reopen at 1800 Eastern, at this edition’s stamp, and no post-open reading stands in the file the desk collected. What stands is the state the reopening inherits. Bitcoin held above the line it retook on Saturday through Sunday’s readings: $61,158 at 11:26 a.m. Eastern, up 2.1 percent on the day, in the warning account filed below; $60,977 at 11:42 UTC in CoinGecko data, in the file’s snapshot readings; and $60,945.06 at 21:55 UTC, on a day that opened at $60,440.01 and ran from $58,768.51 to $61,669.99, in the exchange account filed below—a reading stamped after this edition’s collection hour, printed as the later instrument it is. Saturday’s completed day closed at $60,215.77 after a low of $55,130, in the same account; the five-session return stands at minus 6.41 percent and the month at minus 25.13 percent, in the same account. The week’s mechanism stands in the file whole: $2.5 billion of leveraged longs wiped out in Saturday’s crash leg in one account’s figure, about $1.8 billion in the liquidation count the desk has carried, and November’s net outflow from the United States spot Bitcoin funds at roughly $3.6 billion, on track for the second-worst month since their launch, in the crash account filed below. The named warning in the evening file is Arthur Hayes’s: if the Nasdaq keeps falling, $50,000 is the next real test, in the warning account, which also records Fidelity’s Jurrien Timmer placing his model’s support near $62,000 and rising. The levels the desks are watching stand in the crash account: $62,000 above, $60,000 the round number, $55,100 Saturday’s low.

The closed markets’ bill stands where the week left it, with the trading desk’s own reading added in the midday file and carried here: Goldman Sachs’ Panic Index at 9 of 10, momentum traders $57 billion sold over the past month and net short about $19 billion, and up to $80.6 billion more that could be sold this week if the slide continues, in the accounts the midday file carried. Friday’s closes stand as the last cash readings: the S&P 500 down 3.70 percent at 6,910.39, the Nasdaq Composite down 5.28 percent at 22,617.73, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 1.93 percent at 48,147.33, in the week’s accounts. The week’s test is dated: Dell’s earnings on Tuesday after the close; the October PCE reading, the second estimate of third-quarter product, durable goods and the Beige Book on Wednesday; markets closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and closing early Friday, in the morning brief filed below. December’s rise stands priced at 88.6 percent for a quarter point in one account’s CME figures and all but fully priced in the week’s others—the desk prints both, as at midday. Settled: the week’s losses and Sunday’s hold above $60,000. Open: the futures’ first hour, and Monday’s open behind it.

The Week Ahead: A Council on Monday, a Short Week’s Test, and a Vote on Sunday

The week ahead carries the North Atlantic Council in Brussels on Monday; the Senate Commerce Committee’s technical answers on the November 13 ground stop, due November 23; Virginia’s measles dashboard on November 24; Alaska’s certification on November 25; Dell’s earnings on Tuesday after the close; the October PCE reading, the second estimate of third-quarter product, durable goods and the Beige Book on Wednesday, in a market week closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and closing early Friday; Spain’s second debate, about November 26, and its general election on November 29, the day the OPEC+ ministers also meet; the House committees’ closed-door interview with Nvidia’s former chief executive on December 1; the Federal Reserve’s decision on December 8 and 9; and the end of government funding after December 11. The Dymer rubble, the Banten count, the Kharg convoy and the Miro G’s refloating carry no dates; they will be filed when they land. The Midnight Watch collects at 0000.

The Cocked Hat

Where the evening’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Bahrain’s target: two Patriot radars at Al-Riffa and Awali, in the Guards’ statement; a purely civilian and industrial site, in the Foreign Ministry’s dismissal; the targets named as Shaikh Isa and Al Juffair, in the Fars agency’s account in the earlier files; and no damage to American personnel or facilities, in the United States official’s word, with no Central Command statement on the radars in the file. On the injured: two, one stable and one critical, in the Interior Ministry’s Sunday correction; none, in its Saturday statement; and no casualties from the interceptions’ shrapnel, in the Defence Force’s account of the interceptions. On the strait’s Sunday: two crossings in the visible counter; 23 ships in the monitor’s 24 hours.  Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 35 items.

 SubjectiveNPR — Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuelsAntalya, Turkey: international climate talks in Antalya broke down in overtime hours over how to address fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming. On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold. The talks ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest climate conference in the history of these summits, and ended with delegates from the European Union rejecting any final outcome that did not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels; Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O’Brien, who spoke for the EU, left the room along with EU Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra. Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who ran the negotiations, said the transition away from fossil fuels is happening regardless of what the United Nations agreements say. Only $142 million in additional funding was pledged at the summit.

 SubjectiveCNN — Global climate summit collapses as countries fail to agree on moving away from fossil fuelsThe COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed Sunday as countries failed to agree to an overarching deal after more than two weeks of contentious negotiations. The breaking point was over fossil fuels. The annual talks, which stretched deep into overtime over the weekend, hold the honor of being the longest COP in history and the first major breakdown since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009. At the final meeting intended to approve the Antalya Pact on Sunday, it became clear there would not be the necessary consensus among the more than 190 countries at the talks; these did not include the United States, which has pulled out of international climate action. The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway were among those that rejected the deal. Darragh O’Brien said the bloc would not endorse a deal that does not even mention fossil fuels. COP31 president Murat Kurum acknowledged support was not there: “We have done our utmost,” he said, but “it is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document.” The first draft of the cover decision called for the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems; all mentions of fossil fuels were stripped out of every subsequent draft, despite a push by more than 100 countries to keep them in. More than 90 countries signed a pledge to ramp up the electrification of their economies.

 SubjectiveReuters — Can climate diplomacy build on the collapse of COP31?The collapse of the COP31 talks in Turkey on Sunday without a political agreement left exhausted negotiators questioning the future of a process that for three decades has led the global fight against climate change. The failure follows weak outcomes at other recent conferences. A major difference from Paris in 2015 was that the United States was still engaged in the climate process then; the Antalya talks, the first since a United Nations report saying the world was set to breach the 1.5-degree threshold, marked the second conference since the United States withdrew from the process. James Fletcher, who led the CARICOM group of Caribbean nations in Antalya, cited the lack of a major power backing a positive outcome as a big issue. Delegates said the need for a multilateral deal to direct the shift towards renewable energy has become less necessary as renewable energy becomes economically compelling, and some saw a positive in the wider refusal to accept a weak deal. The determination of big oil producers, led by Saudi Arabia, to block language on fossil fuels arguably reflected the scale of progress achieved. Other forums named include the Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels, the Green Grids Initiative, the Global Methane Pledge and the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance.

 SubjectivePhys.org, carrying AFP — COP31 fails to agree on climate deal in chaotic finaleThe COP31 climate talks headed for a historic defeat Sunday after the European Union and other countries refused to endorse a pact that omitted fossil fuels, as the summit lurched into record overtime in Antalya, 44 hours after its official close. “We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change,” the Union’s negotiators said. COP31 President Murat Kurum conceded the deal had failed to reach consensus: “I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted.” Threats of a walkout Saturday prompted Turkey and Australia to convene a hurried meeting between the European Union and Saudi Arabia, but a compromise remained elusive. The latest text introduced an oblique reference to a previous global deal in 2023 to shift the world away from fossil fuels but stopped short of naming them explicitly, and proposed retaining a push to expand carbon capture. COP31 is now the longest-ever United Nations climate change conference.

 SubjectiveThe Wall Street Journal — U.N. Climate Talks Collapse Over Fossil Fuel RiftUnited Nations climate talks collapsed on Sunday after Europe and nations seeking more ambitious policies refused to accept a deal that did not call for economies to move away from burning fossil fuels. Negotiators met in Antalya on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast for the past two weeks. This year they were facing an energy shock from the Iran war that left much of the world reeling from higher prices, which made developing countries more reluctant to back a deal that would limit investment in new supplies of oil, natural gas and coal, analysts said. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuel either,” Darragh O’Brien, climate minister of Ireland, which holds the European Union’s rotating presidency, said. Excluding mention of fossil fuels would have reversed a deal struck three years ago in Dubai that calls for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly and equitable manner. The talks were also hamstrung by gridlock over setting a global target for wealthy nations to provide funds for the developing world to adapt.

 SubjectiveAND Magazine — Morning Brief, 22 November 2026The Guards said Saturday that it struck two United States Patriot air-defense radars at bases in Bahrain with missiles and drones, calling it a response to United States drone incursions; Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted a number of projectiles and that the attack set fire to a civilian industrial facility, injuring two people. The brief’s week ahead lists Dell earnings Tuesday after the close; PCE, GDP, durable goods and the Beige Book on Wednesday; and markets closed Thursday for Thanksgiving.

 SubjectiveBrussels Reporter — Salvage Operation Begins After Cargo Ship GroundingThe Miro G remains stranded off the Landes coast, her ballast tanks filled with seawater to improve her stability, her two main generators failed and engineers working to restore an alternative supply. The salvage tug Abeille Bretagne is in the area with its 1,000-metre towline and cannot approach closer than about 900 metres in the shallow water. The ship carries no cargo; the pollution risk is her fuel, a little over a hundred tonnes of diesel. No pollution has been detected. Officials said refloating could take several days or longer, and no account promises success at the first weather window.
